case_study_insert.main_stem: Swiftroute Couriers (SRC) is a private limited company in the parcel delivery and express logistics sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 2015 by Daniel Swift, the business delivers same-day parcels for retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. SRC plans to invest $780,000 in an electric van fleet and a sorting hub, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $5 a unit and a selling price of $12, and delivers 50,000 units a year. SRC faces two problems: 8% of parcels arrive late and absenteeism among van drivers is rising during peak periods.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: SRC delivered 13,000 parcels last quarter with 8% arriving late, down from 12% a year earlier. Damage complaints fell from 51 to 29 per month. Average delivery time is 1.4 days. A survey of 500 online shoppers found 69% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed same-day delivery, and 57% choose couriers on reliability. A skills audit shows 30 of 140 drivers lack electric-van training; courses cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Swiftroute Couriers for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (December 2025): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing interest on SRC's $480,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour, affecting SRC's 140 drivers and sorters. (3) Electric-van battery and charging costs rose 8.6% year-on-year while fuel duty increased 3.2% and consumer spending on delivery services grew 4.7%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for SRC of financing its $780,000 sorting-hub expansion with retained profit instead of the $480,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $300,000 needs no interest or repayment, which protects cash flow while SRC already meets fixed costs of $280,000 a year and has a $480,000 loan commitment. With 8% of parcels late and absenteeism rising among van drivers, the cash saved from interest charges can fund the $750 training courses and extra sorting capacity, helping protect the $12 price and the 69% of shoppers who will pay $1.50 more for reliable same-day delivery.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids collateral and repossession risk, so the $780,000 electric vans and sorting hub are safe even if parcel volumes fall short of the 50,000-unit target. It also keeps control with Daniel Swift and the existing team: no lender can attach conditions to how the flat, democratic business runs its routes. That freedom matters when responding quickly to the 57% of shoppers who choose a courier on reliability, since service improvements can be made without seeking a lender's approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to SRC's financing choice and case data.

questions.question_text: SRC is promoting its guaranteed same-day delivery service. Consider sponsoring a city delivery event, local radio advertising, or a targeted email campaign to online retailers. Which should SRC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Sponsoring a city delivery event: A high-profile event builds brand visibility and lets SRC demonstrate vans and speed directly to the public. It suits a same-day service and can generate word of mouth. However, sponsorship is expensive for a business with fixed costs of $280,000 and a $480,000 loan, and the audience includes many people who never buy parcel delivery, so the spend is poorly targeted and results are hard to measure.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper than sponsorship and can repeat a simple reliability message, which matters because 57% of the 500 surveyed shoppers choose a courier on reliability. Its weakness is that listeners are a broad local audience while SRC's customers are online retailers, and radio cannot convey the $1.50 same-day premium clearly or prove that parcels arrive on time.

Targeted email campaign: An email to SRC's retailer contacts reaches the exact businesses that buy same-day delivery, can quote the 69% finding that shoppers will pay $1.50 more, and is cheap and measurable through replies and conversions. It can be personalised by retailer and adjusted quickly. The limits are that it will not build broad consumer awareness and inboxes are crowded, so the offer must be clear and timely.

Recommendation: SRC should choose the targeted email campaign. It reaches the retailers who commission deliveries, supports the $1.50 premium and costs little, while sponsorship is rejected as costly and untargeted and radio as too broad for a retailer-focused service. SRC can add small event sponsorship later once the $780,000 hub is operating.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to SRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SRC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with case figures and a justified recommendation explaining why sponsorship and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: SRC's late-delivery rate is 8% and absenteeism among van drivers is rising. Explain two benefits for SRC of using democratic leadership to improve performance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 140 employees a say in how routes and sorting shifts are organised, so drivers can report the real causes of the 8% late deliveries. In a flat structure their suggestions reach Daniel Swift quickly, and staff who help design the solution are more likely to follow it, reducing late parcels from the current 1.4-day average delivery time and protecting the $12 price.

Point 2: Consulting drivers about the causes of absenteeism makes them more committed and reduces the disruption of peak periods. The audit shows 30 of 140 drivers lack electric-van training, and involving them in planning the $750 courses makes the change feel supportive. Lower absenteeism keeps the 50,000-unit delivery target on track and protects the $7 contribution per parcel from the extra overtime that staff shortages would cause. Clear direction from Daniel Swift also helps co-ordinate the 30 drivers needing training, so absence and lateness are tackled together rather than in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to SRC's delivery, absence and training data.

questions.question_text: SRC wants to reduce rising absenteeism among van drivers. Consider an attendance bonus or job rotation between driving and sorting tasks. Which should SRC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Attendance bonus: A cash bonus for perfect attendance gives drivers a direct financial incentive to turn up, which could quickly reduce the absence that worsens the 8% late-delivery rate during peaks. It is simple to run and links cost to results. The drawbacks are that it rewards attendance rather than effort, can encourage people to work while unwell, and adds a new payment on top of fixed costs of $280,000 a year; the insert gives no pay data, so the size of bonus needed cannot be calculated.

Job rotation: Moving drivers between driving and sorting tasks reduces boredom and stretches skills, addressing the root of absenteeism and the 30 drivers lacking electric-van training by giving them varied experience. It supports the flat, democratic culture and can be introduced without a new wage bill. The weaknesses are that rotation needs training time, may initially slow the 1.4-day delivery average, and sorting staff may resist extra driving duties.

Decision: SRC should choose job rotation, supported by the $750 electric-van courses. It tackles the cause of disengagement rather than paying workers to attend, needs no new payment the insert cannot quantify, and builds flexibility that helps the 50,000-unit target. The attendance bonus is rejected because it would mask the problem and add unquantified cost, though a small bonus could be reconsidered if absence remains high after rotation is established. Managers should monitor absence after rotation begins and keep the 1.4-day delivery average as the test of whether the change is working, adjusting shifts if late parcels rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to SRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options using SRC's absence, lateness and training data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both options with a justified decision on job rotation and clear reasons why the attendance bonus is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SRC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($12 − $5) = $280,000 ÷ $7 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 parcels a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12 − $5 = $7. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SRC's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 40,000-unit break-even point with the 50,000 parcels delivered, giving a margin of safety of 10,000 units, so managers know how far volumes can fall before the sorting hub makes a loss.
2. Use the $7 contribution to evaluate the $1.50 premium that 69% of surveyed shoppers will pay for same-day delivery, testing whether a higher effective price lowers break-even.
3. Check that the $480,000 bank loan and the $780,000 investment are serviceable: above 40,000 parcels each unit adds $7 toward the $280,000 fixed costs and the $120,000 interest payable in the accounts.
4. Track average total cost of $10.60 a parcel ($280,000 ÷ 50,000 + $5) each quarter to spot the cost of the 8% late deliveries and judge the 8.6% rise in electric-van charging costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 parcels | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 10,000 parcels against 50,000 delivered; the $1.50 same-day premium from the 69% survey result; loan-service feasibility on $480,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.60 to track late deliveries and charging costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SRC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SRC's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 25.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 28.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 13.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 14.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $1,500,000 divided by revenue of $6,000,000 gives 25.0%; 2025 gross profit of $1,960,000 divided by $7,000,000 gives 28.0%. Operating profit of $600,000 divided by 2024 revenue gives 10.0%; 2025 operating profit of $910,000 divided by $7,000,000 gives 13.0%. Return on capital employed of $600,000 on $5,000,000 capital gives 12.0%; 2025 return of $910,000 on $6,500,000 gives 14.0%. Revenue rose 16.7% while cost of sales rose 12.0%, and operating profit rose just over 50% while capital employed rose 30%.

Evaluation: Profitability improved on all three measures. The gross margin increased from 25.0% to 28.0% because revenue grew faster than cost of sales, suggesting SRC controlled delivery costs despite the 8% late-delivery problem. Operating return improved from 10.0% to 13.0%, showing the $280,000 fixed costs were spread over more parcels. Returns on capital rose from 12.0% to 14.0%, which is encouraging because capital employed grew to $6,500,000 as the $780,000 sorting-hub plan developed. Interest payable rose from $100,000 to $120,000, yet operating profit grew much faster, so the $480,000 loan has not damaged performance. The figures are historic, however, and do not include the 6.4% wage rise in Appendix 3, which matters for a labour-intensive courier.

Conclusion: SRC's profitability has improved, and the improvement is genuine because both trading margins and the return on the larger capital base rose together. The main risk is that a 28.0% gross margin could be squeezed by wage and charging costs, so management should defend the $7 contribution per parcel and address the 8% late deliveries.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or trends with little or no accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with some relevant analysis of the trends.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SRC of guaranteeing same-day delivery to online shoppers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 500 shoppers found that 69% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed same-day delivery and that 57% choose a courier on reliability. SRC can add $1.50 to the $12 price, raising the $7 contribution per parcel and helping service the $480,000 loan and the $780,000 hub investment. A reliable guarantee also directly targets the 8% late-delivery rate that currently undermines customer confidence.

Disadvantage: A same-day promise requires spare van capacity, tighter sorting schedules and possibly overtime, which pushes up the $280,000 fixed costs and may raise the $5 variable cost per parcel. With absenteeism rising among van drivers, missing the guarantee would disappoint the 69% who paid the premium and could trigger refunds. The extra revenue may therefore be absorbed by operating costs before the electric vans deliver savings. SRC should check that the $1.50 premium covers the extra sorting cost before extending the guarantee to the retailers behind all 500 surveyed shoppers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed development using SRC's survey, cost and delivery data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in electric-van battery and charging costs will affect SRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If SRC's $480,000 loan is variable-rate, the interest increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year. This is small against fixed costs of $280,000 and interest payable of $120,000, and can be removed by fixing the rate. It raises the cost of future borrowing for the $780,000 hub but is otherwise limited.

Electric-van charging cost rise (8.6%): The insert does not split the $5 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of it were energy, 8.6% × $5 = $0.43 per parcel, and at 50,000 parcels that is 50,000 × $0.43 = $21,500 a year. Any real effect is smaller because the variable cost also covers other items, and fuel duty up 3.2% partly offsets the switch to electric vans. The $7 contribution would shrink only modestly.

Minimum wage increase (6.4% to $13.94): SRC has 140 drivers and sorters and delivers 50,000 parcels, so productivity is 50,000 ÷ 140 = 357.1 parcels per worker. Hours and individual pay are not given, so an exact wage-bill total cannot be invented; the correct test is whether productivity holds near 357 parcels per worker. Unlike the interest change, this rise cannot be hedged, and unlike the energy upper bound it is not confined to the $5 variable cost: it applies to the whole workforce of a labour-intensive courier.

Conclusion: The 6.4% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It affects all 140 staff, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate, and is not limited to a fraction of the $5 variable cost as the 8.6% energy rise is; on the evidence available it poses the largest recurring cost pressure. The energy rise ranks second at up to $21,500, and the $3,600 interest rise ranks third.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SRC's costs or financing using case figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown arithmetic, a justified greatest-impact judgement on the wage rise, and reasons why the other two are smaller.
